prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Pre-trained Model (PTM) based Continual Learning (CL) methods face a rigid dichotomy in handling non-stationary data streams. Approaches relying on a **fixed set** of learnable parameters (adapters or prompts) often suffer from limited capacity, restricting their ability to learn novel concepts (plasticity). Conversely, approaches that blindly add **task-specific modules** for every new task suffer from linear model growth and poor knowledge reuse, as they fail to recognize when new tasks share underlying features with previous ones. There is a lack of adaptive mechanisms that can automatically determine *when* and *where* model capacity needs to be expanded based on the data distribution itself, rather than arbitrary task boundaries.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve a sub-linear expansion rate and superior knowledge reuse by decoupling model growth from task identifiers. By equipping each adaptation module with a self-supervised "novelty detector," the model can autonomously assess whether incoming data falls within the distribution of existing knowledge. We posit that expansion should only occur **on demand**—specifically, when the model detects a significant distribution shift that cannot be handled by existing modules—thereby allowing the system to balance stability and plasticity dynamically without catastrophic forgetting.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose **Self-Expansion with Modularized Adaptation (SEMA)**. Our approach moves away from static pools or purely task-dependent growth. Instead, we treat the PTM as a frozen backbone and inject "Modular Adapters" at various layers. The lifecycle of the model is governed by the following logic:

**1. The Modular Adapter Unit**
We redefine the standard adapter into a composite unit consisting of two parts:
*   **The Functional Adapter:** A learnable module designed to adjust feature representations to solve the downstream task (the "actor").
*   **The Representation Descriptor (RD):** A companion module trained to model the density or distribution of the features that the Functional Adapter is trained on (the "sensor").

**2. On-Demand Expansion Logic**
During the training stream, the model scans incoming features at each layer using the existing Representation Descriptors.
*   **Novelty Detection:** Each RD calculates how well it "recognizes" the current input (e.g., via reconstruction quality).
*   **Expansion Trigger:** If *all* existing RDs at a specific layer indicate that the input is out-of-distribution (a novel pattern), the system triggers an expansion signal. A new Modular Adapter (Functional + RD) is instantiated and trained.
*   **Reuse Strategy:** If the input is recognized by existing RDs, no new parameters are added. The system reuses the frozen, existing adapters, facilitating knowledge transfer.

**3. Training and Freezing**
When expansion occurs, we train the new Functional Adapter to minimize the task error and the new RD to capture the new feature distribution. Once trained, these modules are frozen to prevent catastrophic forgetting.

**4. Expandable Weighting Router**
To synthesize the outputs of multiple adapters, we maintain a dynamic routing mechanism. This router acts as a "Mixture of Experts" gate. It learns to assign importance weights to the available adapters based on the input. Crucially, this router is also expandable; as new adapters are added, the router grows to accommodate the new pathways, learning to mix old and new knowledge effectively.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Dynamic Architecture Search:** We provide a mechanism where the model structure evolves autonomously based on data complexity rather than manual design or fixed task sequences.
*   **Efficiency:** We anticipate **sub-linear model growth**, as the system will reuse existing modules for similar tasks rather than creating redundant parameters.
*   **Stability-Plasticity Balance:** By freezing learned modules and only adding new ones for truly novel distributions, we aim to eliminate catastrophic forgetting while maintaining high adaptability.
*   **Representation-Level Control:** The introduction of Representation Descriptors offers a novel way to interpret and control the internal expansion of deep networks based on intermediate feature distributions.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed SEMA (Self-Expansion of pre-trained models with Modularized Adaptation) method against state-of-the-art baselines in a Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) setting.

*   **Model Architecture:**
    *   **Backbone:** Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) pre-trained on ImageNet-1K.
    *   **Backbone Status:** All backbone parameters were kept frozen.
    *   **Adapter Configuration:** We used modular adapters consisting of a functional adapter (projection down/up with ReLU) and a representation descriptor (Autoencoder-based).
    *   **Adapter Hidden Dimension:** 16.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **CIFAR-100:** Split into incremental tasks.
    *   **ImageNet-R (IN-R):** Evaluated with 5-Task, 10-Task, and 20-Task splits.
    *   **ImageNet-A:** Contains adversarial samples.
    *   **VTAB:** Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Average Accuracy ($\bar{\mathcal{A}}$):** The average accuracy throughout the incremental phases.
    *   **Last-Step Average Accuracy ($\mathcal{A}_N$):** The average accuracy after learning all tasks (reflecting the final accumulated knowledge).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **FT Adapter:** Fully fine-tuning the adapter.
    *   **L2P:** Learning to Prompt.
    *   **DualPrompt:** Complementary prompting.
    *   **CODA-P:** Continual Decomposed Attention-based Prompting.
    *   **SimpleCIL:** Simple baseline for CIL.
    *   **ADAM:** With Adapter configuration.
    *   **InfLoRA:** Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Batch Size:** 32.
    *   **Optimizer:** SGD.
    *   **Learning Rates:** Initialized at 0.005 for adapters and 0.01 for Representation Descriptors (RDs).
    *   **Scheduler:** Cosine annealing decay.
    *   **Self-Expansion Scope:** By default, self-expansion was enabled in the last three transformer layers (Layers 10, 11, and 12).
    *   **Expansion Strategy:** Task-oriented expansion; samples were scanned in the first epoch to determine if expansion was necessary based on a Z-score threshold of reconstruction errors.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Incremental Performance Analysis:**
*   We observed that SEMA consistently outperformed baselines in accuracy throughout the incremental learning steps across CIFAR, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, and VTAB datasets.
*   On datasets containing adversarial samples (ImageNet-A) and significant distribution shifts (ImageNet-R), SEMA showed a larger performance margin compared to baselines, while gaps were narrower on CIFAR-100.
*   The performance curves indicated better stability-plasticity balance, as accuracy degradation over time was less severe than in methods like FT Adapter or DualPrompt.

**Dynamic Expansion Dynamics (Reconstruction Error Analysis):**
*   We tracked the reconstruction error of the Representation Descriptors (RDs) during training on the VTAB dataset.
*   We observed that reconstruction error for a specific RD decreased and converged when trained on its corresponding task.
*   When a new task arrived, expansion signals were triggered only when the Z-scores of reconstruction errors from *all* previous RDs were high.
*   Specifically, expansion was triggered for Tasks 1, 2, and 3. Conversely, Tasks 4 and 5 did not trigger expansion, implying that the existing modules (from Tasks 1 and 3) were sufficient to handle the new data distributions.

**Adapter Usage and Reusability:**
*   We visualized the average adapter usage for VTAB tasks.
*   Tasks that triggered expansion (Tasks 1, 2, 3) primarily utilized the adapters specifically trained for them.
*   Tasks that did not trigger expansion (Tasks 4 and 5) demonstrated clear knowledge reuse; Task 4 primarily reused Adapter 1, and Task 5 primarily reused Adapter 3, aligning with the distribution similarities detected by the RDs.

**Expansion Threshold Sensitivity:**
*   We analyzed the impact of varying the Z-score expansion threshold (ranging from 1.0 to 2.0 and 1 to 8 in separate sweeps).
*   We observed that accuracy remained stable despite variations in the threshold, indicating robustness in the Z-score-based signal.
*   Lower thresholds resulted in a higher number of adapters being added (more frequent expansion), while very high thresholds (>1.5) reduced the number of adapters but led to a drop in accuracy due to insufficient adaptation.
*   A wide range of thresholds provided a good balance between performance and model size.

**Multi-Layer Expansion Analysis:**
*   We compared expanding modules in the last 2, 3, and 4 transformer layers.
*   Expanding across multiple layers (e.g., layers 10-12) yielded better accuracy than restricting expansion to fewer final layers.
*   However, extending expansion to earlier layers (e.g., layer 9) significantly increased the total number of added adapters without providing a proportional boost in performance, suggesting that earlier layers behave similarly despite distribution shifts.

**Parameter Efficiency:**
*   We tracked the cumulative number of parameters added as tasks progressed on ImageNet-A.
*   SEMA demonstrated a sub-linear growth rate in parameters relative to the number of tasks.
*   In contrast, task-specific expansion methods (like CODA-P) exhibited linear parameter growth. SEMA's growth was significantly lower than CODA-P and DualPrompt, while being slightly higher than fixed-parameter methods like L2P (which perform worse in accuracy).

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

```latex
  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current approaches to Continual Learning (CL) using Pre-trained Models (PTMs) face a critical dichotomy regarding the stability-plasticity balance. Most existing methods rely on restricted adaptation using a fixed set of learnable modules (adapters or prompts) shared across all tasks; while this mitigates catastrophic forgetting, it severely limits the model's ability to learn novel patterns (plasticity) once the fixed capacity is saturated. Conversely, methods that periodically add task-specific modules result in a linear growth rate of the model size relative to the number of tasks, which is inefficient and impairs the reuse of previously learned knowledge. There is currently no robust mechanism that automatically determines *when* and *where* to expand the model capacity based on the actual data distribution shift, leading to either under-fitting (fixed capacity) or parameter bloating (linear expansion).

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **SEMA** (Self-Expansion of pre-trained models with Modularized Adaptation). Our core hypothesis is that we can achieve sub-linear model growth and superior knowledge transfer by decoupling the adaptation mechanism into "Modular Adapters."

By pairing a functional adapter (for feature transformation) with a **Representation Descriptor (RD)** (for distribution density estimation), the system can autonomously detect distribution shifts at specific layers of the network. We hypothesize that expansion should only occur when the RDs indicate that the incoming data pattern is significantly distinct from previously learned distributions. Furthermore, we propose that these adapters should not be mutually exclusive; instead, we will implement an **Expandable Weighting Router** to learn a soft mixture of experts (MoE), allowing the model to compose existing and new adapters dynamically for any given input.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a PTM-based framework (specifically using a frozen Vision Transformer backbone) that supports self-expansion at arbitrary layers. The methodology consists of three core components: the Representation-Aware Modular Adapter, the Expandable Weighting Router, and the Self-Expansion Strategy.

### 1. Representation-Aware Modular Adapter
We will design the modular adapter as a tuple $( f_{\phi}(\cdot), g_{\varphi}(\cdot) )$, containing a functional adapter and a representation descriptor.

**Functional Adapter ($f_{\phi}$):**
We will insert functional adapters as side branches to the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) modules within the transformer layers. Let $\mathbf{x}^l \in \mathbb{R}^d$ denote the input feature to the MLP at the $l$-th layer. The $k$-th functional adapter $f_{\phi_k^l}(\cdot)$ will bridge the representation gap for downstream tasks. We will formulate this as a bottleneck architecture containing a down-projection $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down},k}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, a ReLU activation, and an up-projection $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up},k}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$.
The output is defined as:
$$ f_{\phi_k^l}(\mathbf{x}^l) = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{x}^l \cdot \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down},k}^l) \cdot \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up},k}^l $$
where $\phi_k^l \equiv \{ \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{up},k}^l, \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{down},k}^l \}$.

**Representation Descriptor ($g_{\varphi}$):**
To enable the module to be aware of local representation distributions, we will pair each functional adapter with a Representation Descriptor (RD), implemented as an Autoencoder (AE). The RD $g_{\varphi_k^l}(\cdot)$ will be trained to reconstruct the features fed into its paired adapter. The objective is to minimize the reconstruction loss on the specific features $\mathcal{X}_k^l$ assigned to adapter $k$:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RD},k}^l(x) = \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X}_k^l} || \mathbf{x} - g_{\varphi_k^l}(\mathbf{x}) ||_2^2 $$
This reconstruction error will serve as a proxy for novelty detection during the expansion phase.

### 2. Expandable Weighting Router
To compose multiple adapters effectively, we will not rely on hard selection. Instead, we will maintain an expandable weighting router $h_{\psi^l}(\cdot)$ at each layer. This router will produce a weighted mixture of the functional adapters.
We define the routing function as a linear mapping followed by a softmax:
$$ \mathbf{w}^l = h_{\psi^l}(\mathbf{x}^l) \equiv \mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{x}^l \cdot \mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{mix}}^l) $$
where $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{mix}}^l \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K^l}$ are the learnable parameters, and $K^l$ is the current number of adapters at layer $l$.

The final output representation of the layer $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}}^l$ will be the sum of the frozen MLP output and the weighted adapter outputs:
$$ \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}}^l = \mathbf{MLP}(\mathbf{x}^l) + \sum_{k=1}^{K^l} w_k^l \cdot f_{\phi_k^l}(\mathbf{x}^l) $$
When a new adapter is added, $\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{mix}}^l$ will be expanded to include a new column, which is trained while existing router parameters are frozen to prevent forgetting.

### 3. Continual Learning Objective
The total objective function will optimize the parameters of the active functional adapters $\{\phi\}$, the router $\{\psi\}$, and the representation descriptors $\{\varphi\}$ across the task sequence. For a task $t$ with dataset $D^t$:
$$ \underset{\{\phi_k^l\}, \{\psi^l\}, \{\varphi_k^l\}}{\operatorname{min}} \mathbb{E}_{(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) \in D^t} \left[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(F_{\{\phi_k^l\}, \{\psi^l\}}(\boldsymbol{x}), \boldsymbol{y}) + \sum_{l=1}^{L} \sum_{k=1}^{K^l} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RD},k}^l(\boldsymbol{x}; \varphi_k^l) \right] $$
where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}$ is the cross-entropy classification loss.

### 4. Self-Expansion Strategy
We will implement a **Z-score based expansion signal**. When a new task arrives, we will scan the samples in the first epoch. We will calculate the reconstruction error $r_k^l$ for an input $\mathbf{x}^l$ using existing RDs. We will maintain running statistics (mean $\mu_k^l$ and standard deviation $\sigma_k^l$) of the reconstruction errors.
The Z-score is calculated as:
$$ z_k^l = \frac{r_k^l - \mu_k^l}{\sigma_k^l} $$
If $z_k^l$ exceeds a predefined threshold for *all* existing adapters $k=1...K^l$ at layer $l$, it indicates a significant distribution shift (novel pattern). This will trigger the instantiation of a new Modular Adapter pair $(f, g)$ at that layer. If the threshold is not met, we reuse the existing adapters.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Automated Architecture Search for CL:** We aim to establish a theoretical framework where the model architecture evolves dynamically based on intrinsic data properties (distribution shifts detected by RDs) rather than extrinsic signals (Task IDs).
2.  **Sub-linear Parameter Growth:** By reusing adapters for tasks with similar feature distributions, we expect the model size to grow significantly slower than linearly relative to the number of tasks.
3.  **Enhanced Stability-Plasticity:** The decoupling of the novelty detection (via RDs) and feature adaptation (via functional adapters) is expected to allow aggressive learning of new tasks without interfering with the weights dedicated to prior stable distributions.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
